title: Wash your feet
hook: thirty nuns take Patacara's teaching while washing their feet (Therigatha, the thirty nuns)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patacara watched a lamp's wick drawn down, nibbana. Your line was the flame goes out. Did you watch one go out, and stay with the dark for a moment? Today, she teaches others, and she starts with their feet. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

Wash your feet, quickly, and sit down to one side. That's the instruction. A group of nuns has come to Patacara, the teacher whose song the path heard yesterday. The collection calls them the thirty nuns, and they have come for teaching. They might expect a long talk, or some hidden method, or a test. What she gives them starts with water and the dust of the road. Today, that instruction, and why a teacher who had been through so much would start there.
screen: `WASH YOUR FEET. SIT DOWN.` → `THE NUNS COME FOR TEACHING.` → `WATER, AND THE ROAD'S DUST.`

segments.voice: First, what she says before the feet. In the poem, Patacara points at young men pounding grain with pestles. They work hard, and with what they earn they keep a household going, wives and children. Effort is ordinary, she's saying. People pour it into a home every day. So pour it into the Buddha's teaching, which, she says, no one regrets. Second, the instruction itself. Wash your feet quickly, sit to one side, give yourself to calm of mind, and do the teaching. No ceremony. The sacred thing and the chore sit in the same sentence. Third, what the nuns do. The poem repeats her words back as deeds. They heard her. They washed their feet. They sat to one side. They gave themselves to calm. Then the night unfolds, watch by watch. In the first, the poem says, they remembered former lives. In the middle, the divine eye was made clear. In the last, they tore through the great mass of darkness. Fourth, the morning. They rise, bow at Patacara's feet, and tell her: we have done what you taught. They say they will honor her the way the thirty gods honor Indra, unbeaten in battle. Notice the shape of it. Patacara's own song tells of washing her feet before her night of release. Now she hands that same small gesture to others, and it serves them too. The water doesn't wake anyone up, and the poem never says it does. It's a doorway. You stop walking. You rinse off the road. You sit.
screen: `PESTLES, GRAIN AND A HOUSEHOLD.` · `WASH QUICKLY, SIT TO ONE SIDE.` · `THE NIGHT, WATCH BY WATCH.` · `BOWING AT HER FEET AT DAWN.` · then, large: `WASH YOUR FEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wash your feet with attention. If you can, do it now, at a tub or a basin. If you can't, your hands will do. Feel the temperature of the water first. Then the weight of the foot, or the hand, under it. Whatever road you walked today, let it go down the drain. Patacara said quickly, and quickly here can mean without fuss, not without care. Then sit to one side, the way the nuns did, dry or damp, and let the breath settle on its own. The bell holds the time.
Pada. The Pali word for foot: Patacara's instruction to the nuns was to wash their feet, rinse off the road, sit to one side, and turn the mind to calm. Today's word.
Your line: rinse off the road. Today, before one thing that matters, a meal, a hard call, a quiet sit, stop and rinse your hands or feet first, and arrive. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist monasteries keep water by the door for washing the feet before entering the hall, and some Theravada teachers read the verses of Patacara and her students as a picture of practice that begins in ordinary acts.

fork.setup: you're one of the nuns who came to Patacara for teaching. she has finished speaking. what do you do?
options: ask her for a longer, deeper teaching.
wash your feet and sit to one side.
go home to think it over.
fork.reveal: the poem repeats her words back as deeds: they washed their feet, sat to one side, and by the last watch of the night had torn through the darkness.

original.note: Pali pada: foot. The nuns wash their feet at night, and in the morning bow at Patacara's.

what it means: Patacara's instruction to her students: rinse off the road, sit to one side, turn to calm. the teaching starts with a chore.
what a scholar hears: the thirty nuns' verses repeat Patacara's words back as deeds, the same steps her own song tells: washing the feet, then sitting through the watches of the night.

notes: All Therigatha material is paraphrased; no translation quoted.
'Thirty' comes from the poem's heading in the collection (Timsamatta theri, 'about thirty'); the script attributes it to the collection. Confirm.

Confirm the paraphrase of Thig 5.11: young men with pestles supporting wives and children; 'wash your feet quickly and sit to one side'; the three watches (past lives, divine eye, mass of darkness); bowing at her feet and the comparison to the gods honoring Indra, unconquered in battle.
The script says Patacara's own song (Thig 5.10) tells of washing her feet before her night of release; confirm.
Original: पाद (pada); confirm Devanagari and pronunciation guide.
